newsitem.title: JAPAN: NTT caught up in global telecom rivalry - sources.
newsitem.headline: NTT caught up in global telecom rivalry - sources.

text.p: Just weeks after being freed to pursue international businesses, Japan's telecom titan NTT Corp seems caught in a scuffle among big European carriers racing to woo the wealthy Asian partner, industry sources say.

"NTT is now at the centre of the global rivalry (among three alliances) to grab more territory," said an industry official close to the company. "NTT is trying hard not to get involved in political struggles."

Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, boasting strong ties with Japanese multinationals and a large presence in Asia, has been tight-lipped about any international tie-ups, but global carriers, particularly from Europe, are said to be aggressively courting NTT to join their own telecom groupings.

At present there are three main global alliances, including Concert, a tie-up between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp of the United States, and Global One, consisting of Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and America's Sprint Corp.
A third alliance is WorldPartners, a loosely-knit organisation assembled by U.S. telecoms giant AT&T.

Industry officials said a media report on Thursday that NTT is exploring a $500 million investment alongside BT in a French carrier may signal the start of some back-room wrangling for NTT's attentions.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that NTT was considering investing $500 million to buy 10 percent of French carrier Cegetel, a unit of Cie Generale des Eaux and the main rival to France Telecom.
NTT said it was not actively considering such a stake.
"We're not in a situation to actively consider any such move. Everything is up in the air," an NTT spokesman said, adding that there were many such investment proposals.

"I see few benefits for NTT in acquiring the stake," said Hirofumi Inada, analyst at Okasan Securities Co. "A possible reason (why the article appeared) is that BT wants to send a message to France Telecom to withdraw from the courtship of NTT."
Some industry officials said a BT-NTT tie-up may be imminent, as regulatory restrictions on NTT's international services would prompt it to seek a global partner.
But they added that any tie-up would probably be limited, not involving joint ventures or the acquisition of shares, and most likely starting with the leasing of phone lines.
Most analysts said, however, that NTT would prefer to wait before choosing a partner.

"There is no need for NTT to pick a partner now since it has the closest links to giant Japanese multinationals and definitely has an edge," said UBS Securities analyst Toshiho Sato. "NTT could set up its own exchange systems in the world's major cities as a first step, and then see what it can do."
NTT, which last month won regulatory approval to offer international services as part of its restructuring, has acquired telecom licenses in Britain, Germany and France.
An NTT official recently told Reuters that any international alliance would be restricted to certain sectors or technologies in which NTT is weak.
"It's very unlikely that NTT would become a full-fledged member of any of the world's three consortiums," he said.
The NTT group already has investments in Thai Telephone and Telecommunications and in other Asian countries, such as the Philippines, Indonesia, India and Vietnam.

The group, jointly with local ventures, also offers cellular phone and paging services in China and India, and has clinched government contracts to build on-line data communications sytems in China, Turkey and Thailand.

NTT president Junichiro Miyazu plans to visit England, Germany, France and the United States in early February to explain the company's restructuring plans to firms it does business with, including BT.
